subject: Medicine
summary: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune synovitis causing joint damage and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern, serology and imaging; early treatment prevents disability.

sections.p: RA is a symmetric polyarthritis with persistent synovial inflammation. Diagnosis uses the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria: joint involvement, serology (RF, anti‑CCP), acute‑phase reactants, symptom duration.
b: ≥6/10 points confirms RA
RF or anti‑CCP positivity increases specificity

t.b: Does the patient have autoantibodies? Positive result supports autoimmune etiology and predicts erosive disease
Is there erosive change? Joint space narrowing and marginal erosions confirm established disease
Is there active synovitis? Detects early inflammation when X‑ray is normal

sections.p: Disease activity is graded by DAS28 or CDAI; radiographic staging (Sharp/van der Heijde) tracks erosions. Functional status uses HAQ.
b: DAS28>5.1 = high activity
Sharp score > 100 = severe radiographic damage

sections.p: RA is multifactorial: genetic predisposition (HLA‑DRB1), smoking, and mucosal citrullination. In low‑resource settings consider co‑existing infections that can trigger or mimic RA.
b: HLA‑DRB1 shared epitope
Smoking amplifies citrullination
TB or hepatitis B can cause reactive arthritis

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and systematic joint exam reveal the pattern, severity and extra‑articular features of rheumatoid arthritis and guide further testing.
b: Onset: gradual weeks‑months versus acute trauma; ask for first joint involved.
Morning stiffness duration – >30 min suggests inflammatory arthritis.
Symmetry: involvement of both hands, wrists, feet; note any asymmetry.
Number of joints: small joints (MCP/PIP) vs large joints; count swollen/tender joints.
Systemic symptoms: fatigue, fever, weight loss, sicca symptoms, nodules, pleurisy, vasculitis.
Medication history: NSAIDs, DMARDs, biologics, steroids, herbal remedies; adherence and side‑effects.
Risk factors: smoking, family history, occupational exposures, infections (TB, hepatitis).

t.b: Look for swelling, erythema, deformities (swan‑neck, boutonnière, ulnar deviation); a positive finding confirms visible inflammation but cannot quantify depth.
Assess tenderness, warmth, effusion; tenderness >2 kg pressure indicates active synovitis; cannot differentiate rheumatoid from septic effusion.
Limited motion with pain suggests joint inflammation; full passive ROM with pain points to tendon involvement; ROM does not grade radiographic damage.
Reduced grip correlates with disease activity; does not replace DAS28.
Ask patient to extend fingers; ulnar deviation >10° indicates chronic RA deformity; cannot assess early disease.
Squeeze MCP joints; pain indicates synovitis; negative test does not rule out early disease.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and imaging studies answer specific diagnostic, prognostic and monitoring questions; alternatives are provided for low‑resource settings.
b: RF and anti‑CCP: detect autoantibodies; anti‑CCP >20 U/mL highly specific for RA; negative does not exclude disease.
Complete blood count: anemia of chronic disease common; leukopenia may signal drug toxicity.
Serum creatinine & LFTs: baseline before DMARDs; elevated values may limit drug choice.
Radiographs of hands/feet: look for periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, erosions; Sharp/van der Heijde score >100 denotes severe damage.
Ultrasound: detects synovial hypertrophy and power‑Doppler flow; useful when X‑ray normal; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam.
MRI (if available): visualises early bone marrow edema; not required for routine care.
Chest X‑ray: screen for rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion; if unavailable, focus on respiratory symptoms.

t.b: Screening test; positive in ~70 % of established RA; low specificity—positive in infections, hepatitis, older age.
Diagnostic test; >20 U/mL gives >90 % specificity; high titres predict erosive disease.
Inflammatory marker; >30 mm/h suggests active disease; normal ESR does not rule out early RA.
Radiographic severity index; score >100 correlates with severe erosive disease; repeat every 1‑2 years.
Detects active synovitis; grade 0‑3 flow; grade ≥2 predicts flare; if ultrasound unavailable, use clinical DAS28.
Identifies interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion, rheumatoid nodules; normal film does not exclude early ILD.

sections.p: Classification relies on the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria; staging uses radiographic scores and disease‑activity indices.
b: Score ≥6/10 points from joint involvement, serology, acute‑phase reactants and symptom duration confirms RA.
Joint involvement: 1 large joint =0, 2–10 small joints =1, >10 small joints (≥1 large) =2.
Serology: negative RF & anti‑CCP =0; low‑positive RF or anti‑CCP =2; high‑positive RF or anti‑CCP =3.
Acute‑phase reactants: normal CRP/ESR =0; abnormal CRP/ESR =1.
Symptom duration: <6 weeks =0; ≥6 weeks =1.
Staging (radiographic): Stage 0 – normal; Stage I – soft‑tissue swelling; Stage II – early erosions; Stage III – extensive erosions, joint space loss; Stage IV – deformity, ankylosis.
Severity (activity): DAS28 ≤3.2 = low; 3.2–5.1 = moderate; >5.1 = high; CDAI ≤10 = low, 10–22 = moderate, >22 = high.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic rheumatoid arthritis; key discriminators are listed to avoid misdiagnosis.

t.b: Asymmetric oligo‑ or polyarthritis, dactylitis, nail pitting, scalp psoriasis; radiographs show pencil‑in‑cup erosions, not uniform MCP involvement.
Positive ANA, anti‑dsDNA, malar rash, renal involvement; arthritis is non‑erosive, often migratory, with low RF.
History of GI or genitourinary infection, asymmetric lower‑limb predominance, sacroiliitis; HLA‑B27 positive, no erosions on early X‑ray.
Joint pain worsens with use, minimal morning stiffness, Heberden’s nodes, joint space narrowing without erosions; radiographs show osteophytes.
Acute mono‑articular pain, fever, high leukocyte count in synovial fluid (>50 000 cells/µL), positive Gram stain; requires urgent drainage.

sections.p: A pragmatic ladder for low‑resource settings that starts with rapid symptom control, moves to disease‑modifying therapy, and escalates based on disease activity, organ involvement and treatment safety.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis, assess disease activity (DAS28, CDAI) and screen for infections (TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV).
2. Begin non‑pharmacologic measures: patient education, joint protection, physiotherapy, smoking cessation, vaccination before immunosuppression.
3. First‑line csDMARD: methotrexate (unless contraindicated). If contraindicated, use leflunomide or sulfasalazine.
4. Add short‑course NSAID or low‑dose glucocorticoid for flare control while DMARD takes effect; taper steroids within 6‑12 weeks.
5. If DAS28 >5.1 after 3‑6 months of optimal csDMARD, add a bDMARD (TNF‑α inhibitor) or a targeted synthetic DMARD (JAK inhibitor) if biologics unavailable.
6. Monitor labs (CBC, LFT, renal) every 3‑6 months; repeat DAS28; obtain X‑ray of hands/feet every 1‑2 years.
7. Escalate to combination csDMARDs or switch biologic class if inadequate response or adverse event; refer to rheumatology centre for refractory disease or extra‑articular complications.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects of the main agents and practical steps to mitigate them, especially where laboratory monitoring is limited.
b: Leflunomide – hepatotoxicity, hypertension, alopecia; perform baseline LFT, avoid in pregnancy, use cholestyramine washout if discontinuation needed.
Sulfasalazine – rash, neutropenia, hepatotoxicity; check CBC and LFT, discontinue if neutrophils <1.0 ×10⁹/L or ALT >3 × ULN.
TNF‑α inhibitors – reactivation of latent TB, serious infection, demyelinating disease; screen for TB and hepatitis B, hold drug during active infection, avoid in uncontrolled demyelination.
JAK inhibitors – venous thromboembolism, herpes zoster, lipid rise; screen for VTE risk, vaccinate against shingles, monitor lipids, avoid in active malignancy.
Glucocorticoids – hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, infection; give calcium/vitamin D, consider bisphosphonate if >3 months, taper promptly, monitor glucose.

sections.p: Recognise organ‑specific complications that demand rapid therapeutic intensification or specialist referral.
b: Rapidly progressive erosive disease (Sharp score rise >5 points/yr) → add or switch to a bDMARD.
New interstitial lung disease or worsening dyspnoea with HRCT fibrosis → stop methotrexate, start cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate, refer to pulmonology.
Renal amyloidosis (proteinuria >1 g/day, low serum albumin) → intensify DMARDs, consider biologic, involve nephrology.
Severe anaemia of chronic disease with ferritin >300 µg/L and low iron → treat active inflammation, evaluate for occult infection.
Vasculitic skin ulcer or neuropathy → add high‑dose steroids and consider cyclophosphamide; urgent rheumatology input.
Persistent pleural effusion with glucose <30 mg/dL → rule out infection, consider DMARD escalation, chest physiotherapy.

sections.p: Conditions and exposures that alter presentation, laboratory interpretation, or therapeutic choices in rheumatoid arthritis.
b: HIV – serology may be false‑negative for RF/anti‑CCP; CD4 <200 cells/µL raises infection risk, prefer csDMARDs, avoid TNF‑α blockers until immune reconstitution.
Active TB – can mimic systemic symptoms; screen with GeneXpert; defer biologics until completion of anti‑TB therapy.
Malnutrition – low albumin skews acute‑phase reactants; supplement protein, use weight‑based dosing for methotrexate, monitor for cytopenias.
Pregnancy – methotrexate and leflunomide are teratogenic; switch to sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine, avoid biologics unless benefits outweigh risks.
Diabetes – glucocorticoids worsen glycaemia; use lowest effective dose, monitor glucose, consider early DMARD escalation to limit steroid exposure.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort) – induce CYP enzymes, lower biologic levels; obtain full medication history, counsel cessation.
Alcohol – potentiates methotrexate hepatotoxicity; limit intake, monitor LFT more frequently.
Renal failure – methotrexate contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min; use leflunomide or low‑dose sulfasalazine, adjust NSAID dosing.

sections.p: Tailored approaches for populations with distinct physiological or socioeconomic considerations.
b: Children (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) – use methotrexate as first csDMARD, avoid leflunomide, consider etanercept; monitor growth, vaccinate before biologics.
Pregnant women – continue sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine, stop methotrexate ≥3 months before conception, use certolizumab if biologic needed (minimal placental transfer).
Elderly – higher infection and renal risk; start methotrexate at low dose, prefer short‑course steroids, avoid JAK inhibitors if VTE risk high.
People with HIV – prioritize csDMARDs, defer TNF‑α blockers until CD4 >350 cells/µL and viral load suppressed; prophylaxis for opportunistic infections.

Low‑resource settings – use methotrexate plus affordable NSAID, rely on clinical DAS28 without ESR if unavailable, obtain X‑ray only when progression suspected, use generic biosimilar TNF inhibitors when needed.

facts: 2010 ACR/EULAR RA classification requires ≥6/10 points; joint involvement, serology, acute-phase reactants, symptom duration
DAS28 >5.1 = high disease activity; 3.2‑5.1 = moderate; ≤3.2 = low/remission
Sharp/van der Heijde score >100 indicates severe radiographic damage
Anti‑CCP specificity >95% for RA; RF sensitivity ~70%
Methotrexate is first‑line csDMARD unless contraindicated
Biologic TNF‑inhibitors added if DAS28 remains >3.2 after 3‑6 months of csDMARD
Smoking increases risk 2‑fold; cessation improves treatment response
Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before initiating biologics

vivas.q: What are the four domains of the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria and their point allocations?
vivas.a: Joint involvement (0‑5), serology (0‑3), acute‑phase reactants (0‑1), symptom duration (0‑1). ≥6 points classifies RA.

vivas.q: Interpret a DAS28 score of 5.6 in a patient on methotrexate for 4 months.
vivas.a: Score >5.1 indicates high disease activity; consider adding a biologic or switching csDMARD.

vivas.q: Why is long‑term NSAID monotherapy discouraged in RA?
vivas.a: NSAIDs relieve pain but do not prevent joint damage and increase GI/renal risk, especially in low‑resource settings without protective agents.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate rheumatoid from psoriatic arthritis on hand X‑ray?
vivas.a: RA shows symmetric marginal erosions and joint space narrowing; PsA shows asymmetric ‘pencil‑in‑cup’ deformities and periostitis.

vivas.q: What bedside test helps assess functional hand impairment in RA?
vivas.a: The grip strength test using a dynamometer; reduced strength correlates with disease activity and joint damage.

vivas.q: A patient on methotrexate develops mouth ulcers. Which cellular deficiency is responsible?
vivas.a: Folate deficiency due to impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing mucosal cells.

vivas.q: Renal biopsy shows apple‑green birefringence with Congo red stain. What pathology does this confirm?
vivas.a: Amyloid deposition (AA amyloidosis) secondary to chronic inflammation.

vivas.q: What is the classic pleural fluid finding in rheumatoid pleuritis?
vivas.a: Low glucose (<30 mg/dL) with high LDH and neutrophil predominance.

vivas.q: Explain the mechanism by which NSAIDs and low‑dose aspirin cause a gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature.
vivas.a: Inhibition of COX‑1 reduces prostaglandin‑mediated mucosal protection, leading to acid‑related erosion, especially on the lesser curvature where blood supply is less robust.

vivas.q: Which syndrome links neutropenia, splenomegaly and rheumatoid arthritis?
Identify the interstitial lung disease pattern seen in RA with uniform fibrosis and no honeycombing.
vivas.a: Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern is typical; however RA often shows nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) with uniform fibrosis.

vivas.q: List the three major hand deformities in established RA and their pathophysiology.
vivas.a: Ulnar deviation (synovitis of MCP), boutonnière (central slip rupture of extensor tendon), swan‑neck (hyperextension of PIP with flexed DIP due to extensor mechanism imbalance).

vivas.q: What are the key extra‑articular vascular manifestations of RA?
vivas.a: Rheumatoid nodules, vasculitis of small/medium vessels, increased atherosclerotic risk leading to myocardial infarction and stroke.

vivas.q: How should you monitor disease activity in a low‑resource setting where DAS28 labs are unavailable?
vivas.a: Use the Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) which relies on tender/swollen joint counts and patient/physician global assessments.

vivas.q: What is the recommended vaccination strategy before starting a biologic DMARD?
vivas.a: Administer inactivated vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B) at least 2 weeks prior; avoid live vaccines while on biologics.

vivas.q: In a pregnant woman with RA, which DMARD is safest to continue?
vivas.a: Hydroxychloroquine; methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped preconception.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify the presentation of RA?
vivas.a: Joint symptoms may be less erosive; serology can be negative; higher infection risk when using biologics necessitates careful screening.

vivas.q: What is the first step if a patient on methotrexate presents with elevated liver enzymes?
vivas.a: Check for other hepatotoxins, counsel alcohol abstinence, repeat LFTs in 4‑6 weeks; consider dose reduction or alternative DMARD if persistent.

mcqs.q: A 48‑year‑old woman with RA on methotrexate develops painful oral ulcers. Which supplement would most likely prevent this side effect?
mcqs.e: Folic acid replenishes folate stores depleted by methotrexate, reducing mucosal toxicity.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most specific serologic test for early RA?
mcqs.e: Anti‑CCP antibodies have >95% specificity for RA, especially early disease.

mcqs.q: A patient with longstanding RA presents with a painless, firm nodule over the olecranon. This finding indicates:
mcqs.e: Rheumatoid nodules are common extra‑articular manifestations; olecranon location is classic.

mcqs.q: Which radiographic feature best distinguishes RA from osteoarthritis?
mcqs.e: Marginal erosions at the joint periphery are characteristic of RA, not OA.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource clinic without access to anti‑CCP testing, which combination of clinical features most strongly suggests RA?
o: Asymmetric large‑joint pain, nocturnal pain, normal ESR
Symmetric small‑joint swelling, morning stiffness >30 min, elevated ESR
mcqs.e: Symmetric small‑joint involvement with prolonged morning stiffness and raised acute‑phase reactants is typical of RA.

mcqs.q: A 62‑year‑old man with RA has a pleural effusion with glucose 22 mg/dL. Which statement is true?
o: It requires immediate thoracentesis for infection control
It is caused by heart failure
mcqs.e: Low glucose pleural fluid is classic for rheumatoid pleuritis due to high metabolic activity of inflammatory cells.

cases.v: 60‑year‑old man with 10‑year RA, on long‑term NSAIDs and low‑dose aspirin, presents with epigastric pain, melena, and a tender ulcer on the lesser curvature on endoscopy.

qs.q: What is the primary pathogenic mechanism of his ulcer?
qs.a: COX‑1 inhibition reduces protective prostaglandins, impairing mucosal defense.

qs.q: Which medication should be stopped or replaced?
qs.a: Discontinue diclofenac; replace NSAID with selective COX‑2 inhibitor if needed, add proton‑pump inhibitor.

qs.q: What preventive strategy is recommended for RA patients requiring chronic NSAIDs?
qs.a: Concurrent use of a proton‑pump inhibitor or misoprostol and testing for H. pylori eradication.

mistakes: Relying solely on RF positivity without considering anti‑CCP or clinical picture
Using DAS28 without ESR/CRP when labs are unavailable; CDAI is preferred
Continuing high‑dose NSAIDs without gastro‑protection in ulcer‑prone patients
Starting biologics without screening for latent TB or hepatitis B
Confusing rheumatoid nodules with infectious abscesses; assess for infection first
Neglecting vaccination before biologic therapy, leading to preventable infections
